Subject: Billing mechanics for streaming long-context (pilot)

Hi Rafael,

Thanks again for the demo today — the latency on long searches looked great. Before we move to a pilot, legal asked a few concrete questions about how you actually bill for a mixture of long-context sync requests and streaming snippet requests. High level questions:

- When a single user session mixes a 40k-context document fetch (one-off) and then many short streaming snippets (200–400 tokens each), how are tokens grouped for billing?
- Is there any rounding up to a minimum per-call or per-session? If so, how does that interact with the pilot discount you proposed?
- We stream partial results to the UI (server-side streaming). Are the streamed tokens counted as they are emitted or only at the end of the call?

Could you provide a couple of concrete examples (numbers) as we pass this to finance? Also attached is the deck you shared — I highlighted the pricing slide and added a few comments.

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.com>

Cc: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Billing mechanics for streaming long-context (pilot)

Hi Elena — great questions. I pulled together a few examples below and outlined how our billing logic applies to mixed workloads. Short answer up front: tokens are metered per-request and streamed tokens are counted at emission; we apply a small per-call floor and then aggregate across the invoice window for minimum smoothing. Your pilot discount applies to the final billed units after rounding/aggregation, not to raw token counts.

Example A — one-off long ingest + short streams (single user session)
- Long fetch: 40,000 context tokens (one request)
- Follow-up streams: 10 streams × 300 tokens emitted each = 3,000 streamed tokens
- Raw tokens = 43,000 tokens

How we meter:
- Each request is tokenized and metered at the time tokens are emitted/finished. For the 40k request, we meter the full 40k when the call completes. For streaming, each chunk emitted is added to the running token count immediately.
- Per-call floor: we have a 50-token minimum per request to avoid microbilling. Any request under 50 tokens is rounded up to 50. (That only affects very short calls.)
- Invoice-window aggregation: during invoice calculation we sum tokens and then apply the context-floor smoothing (if you enabled smoothing). By default smoothing is ON for pilots — it consolidates small per-call rounding to avoid excessive rounding overhead.

Billing math (no smoothing, baseline pricing for example):
- Raw tokens = 43,000
- Per-call floors: only applies if any request < 50 tokens (none here)
- Final billed tokens = 43,000
- Pilot discount (example) = 20% off billed token spend (applied post-aggregation)

Example B — many micro streams + occasional long call (shows rounding effects)
- 500 streams × 35 tokens each = 17,500 tokens (but each stream hits the 50-token floor)
- One long call: 10,000 tokens
- Raw tokens = 27,500

How floor affects this:
- Each of the 500 small streams is rounded up to 50 tokens = billed 500 × 50 = 25,000 tokens (instead of 17,500)
- Long call billed at 10,000
- Final billed tokens = 35,000 (before invoice-window smoothing)
- If smoothing is enabled we look at the invoice window and can apply an offset credit for repeated floors; smoothing logic reduces the effective impact of repeated small-call floors.

Streaming timing: tokens are counted as emitted. Reason: it avoids double-counting when clients cancel mid-stream and gives accurate metering for partial outputs.

Pilot discount behavior:
- Pilot discount is applied to the billed token units for the invoice period (post-floor, post-smoothing).
- If we agree a committed seat or reserved capacity for the pilot, we can apply a blended effective rate for the committed portion and standard metered rates for overage.

Follow-ups / asks:
1) Do you want smoothing ON for this pilot? It reduces the impact of microstreams on your bill but slightly increases complexity in reporting (we provide line-item breakdowns).
2) If you expect lots of microstreams we should discuss a per-call floor waiver or a small per-month credit as a concession for pilots. I looped in Vanessa and Karthik to advise on concession authority and the deal packaging.

Attached: short worked examples and a one-page math summary. Happy to hop on a quick call to walk finance through the numbers.

Best,
Rafael Mendes
Account Executive, Enterprise Sales
Redwood Inference
Attachment: pilot-billing-examples.pdf

Vanessa / Karthik — Elena asked for clarity on floors and streaming. I sent the worked examples (attached). Two asks from their side:

1) Turn smoothing ON for the pilot (recommended). That should cut the microstream floor overhead by ~60% in our sample workload.
2) A small one-time pilot credit to mitigate the heavy impact if smoothing cannot be enabled on their side (they have strict audit traceability requirements). They asked for ~USD 1,500 of pilot credit to cover first month round-up exposure.

My recommendation: approve smoothing ON (no problem) + approve a one-time USD 1,000 credit (compromise). This keeps list-price integrity while showing good faith. If we want to cap credits, we can add a clause that credits only apply to metered tokens (not committed capacity).

Notes:
- Workload pattern: a mix of many short streams and occasional long fetches — fits the example B profile.
- Region: US, no cross-region routing.

If you approve I will send a revised pilot SOW with smoothing flag and the credit line called out.

Thanks,
Rafael
